opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say we're at a genuinely exciting but also somewhat overhyped moment. On the hardware side, the progress has been remarkable. Actuators are getting better and cheaper, battery density is improving, and you're seeing a lot of companies converge on designs that can walk reliably, balance, and handle basic manipulation. A few years ago, getting a bipedal robot to walk across uneven terrain without falling was a research milestone. Now it's almost table stakes.

The real bottleneck, in my view, is still on the intelligence and dexterity side. Hands are incredibly hard. The human hand has an enormous number of degrees of freedom, rich tactile sensing, and the ability to adapt grip on the fly. Most humanoids today can do a decent job with structured pick-and-place tasks, but put them in a messy, unstructured environment, like a real home or a cluttered warehouse floor, and performance drops off quickly.

What's changed is that the large foundation model approach is starting to bleed into robotics. People are training vision-language-action models on large amounts of teleoperation data, simulation, and video, and that's producing robots that generalize better than the hand-coded systems of the past. But we're data-constrained in a way that language models never were. There's no internet-scale corpus of robot interaction data, so a lot of the race right now is really about who can collect high-quality physical data most efficiently.

So my honest take is that the demos are ahead of the deployments. You'll see impressive videos, but the number of humanoids doing useful, paid work, eight hours a day, reliably, is still small. I think the next few years are going to be about closing that gap: proving out narrow commercial use cases in logistics and manufacturing, driving down cost, and building the data flywheel. The general-purpose household humanoid is coming, but it's further out than a lot of the headlines suggest.

r002.rationale: It calls hands “incredibly hard” and describes limitations in humanoids’ hand dexterity, presenting this as a broad unresolved challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say we're at a genuinely interesting inflection point, but with a lot of hype layered on top of it.

On the hardware side, the progress over the last few years has been real. Actuators have gotten cheaper and more capable, battery density has improved, and the cost of building a bipedal platform that can walk reliably has come way down. You've got Tesla, Figure, Agility, Apptronik, Unitree, and a dozen others all shipping or demoing machines that would have looked like science fiction a decade ago. So the body is getting there.

The harder problem, and the one I think people underestimate, is the brain. Walking is mostly solved. Manipulation is not. Picking up an arbitrary object you've never seen before, in a cluttered environment, with the right amount of force, and then doing something useful with it, that's still really difficult. The foundation model approach has helped enormously. You're seeing these vision-language-action models that let a robot generalize from demonstrations in ways that weren't possible before. But the data problem is brutal. Language models trained on the whole internet. Robots don't have an internet's worth of physical interaction data to learn from, so everyone's scrambling with teleoperation, simulation, and synthetic data to close that gap.

Then there's the economics. The demo videos are impressive, but the question is whether you can get a humanoid to do a job reliably, for eight or sixteen hours a day, at a cost that beats a human or a purpose-built machine. Right now the honest answer is mostly no, with a few narrow exceptions in logistics and manufacturing where the tasks are repetitive and the environment is controlled.

So my overall take is that the trajectory is real and I'm optimistic about the direction, but the timelines you hear from some CEOs are aggressive. I'd expect meaningful deployment in warehouses and factories over the next few years, and the general-purpose home robot is further out than the marketing suggests.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re at a really exciting stage, but there’s a big gap between a humanoid doing something impressive in a demo and a robot doing useful work reliably every day. The demo shows you what’s possible. Deployment tells you whether it’s actually a product.

Humanoids have an appealing premise: we’ve built our world around the human body, so a robot with a similar form could work in those spaces. But you’re also taking on a tremendous amount of complexity—balance, manipulation, power, safety—all at once.

For me, the question is: what job does it need to do, and does it need a human shape to do it? If you can solve that problem with a simpler machine, that’s often the better starting point. I’m optimistic about humanoids, but I’d judge progress by how much useful work they can do without someone stepping in.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re at a really exciting stage, but there’s still a big gap between a compelling demonstration and a robot that can do useful work reliably. You can get a humanoid to perform a task in a controlled environment. The harder question is: Can it do that task all day, safely, around people, and at a cost that makes sense?

The human form has an obvious appeal because we’ve built our environments around people. But that doesn’t mean every job needs two legs and two arms. I’d start with the problem you’re trying to solve and work backward to the right machine. Humanoids will have a role, but I think the real measure of progress is going to be deployments that deliver consistent value.
